items.q: A third-party cookie is set by a site other than the one the visitor is on.
items.why: A first-party cookie belongs to the site being visited. A third-party cookie belongs to someone else.

items.q: A first-party cookie is set by the site the visitor is actually on.
items.why: It is often used for logins and remembering preferences.

items.q: Mobile advertising IDs and cookies work in exactly the same way in every browser and app.
items.why: They are different identifiers with different rules and controls.

items.q: A data clean room lets two parties match data without handing over raw personal records.
items.why: Only agreed, combined results leave the clean room.

items.q: An identity graph links different identifiers that belong to the same person or household.
items.why: It helps recognise someone across devices and channels.

items.q: Deterministic matching uses known information such as a login, while probabilistic matching uses estimates.
items.why: Deterministic matches are more certain. Probabilistic ones are guesses with a confidence level.

items.q: First-party data is data a company collects directly from its own audience.
items.why: Sign-ups, purchases and logins are examples.

items.q: Universal IDs work the same way everywhere, whatever consent the person gave.
items.why: Whether an ID can be used still depends on the person’s choices and the local rules.

items.q: People can delete or block cookies in their browser.
items.why: That is why cookie-based recognition is never perfectly reliable.

items.q: Data onboarding connects offline customer records to online identifiers.
items.why: It lets a brand reach people it already knows from, say, a loyalty card.
